I ask to use the phone at the reception desk and, as I dial Jack\u2019s number, I tell Mr Ho that although Jack had warned me he might only be able to take the Wednesday evening flight, I can\u2019t help feeling worried because he would have phoned to let me know. When I get through to his voicemail, my voice is shaky with tears of disappointment and frustration. \u2018Jack, where are you? I know the flight was delayed, but you should be here by now. I hope it doesn\u2019t mean that you\u2019re not arriving until tomorrow\u2014if that\u2019s the case, you could have at least warned me. Have you any idea how worrying it is to be without any news from you for the last four days? Even if you didn\u2019t want to answer your phone you could have phoned me, you must have got all my messages. Please give me a ring, Jack, it\u2019s awful being stuck here not knowing what\u2019s happening\u2014not that I\u2019m not being well looked after,\u2019 I add hurriedly, aware that Mr Ho is listening, \u2018because I am, but I just want you here. Please phone and tell me what\u2019s happening\u2014I\u2019m in the lobby now, but I\u2019ll be going back up to my room, or you can leave a message with Mr Ho at reception. I love you.\u2019 I hang up to find Mr Ho looking sympathetically at me. He suggests that I go through for breakfast and, when I tell him that I\u2019m not hungry, he promises to call me if Jack phones, so I let him persuade me to have something to eat. As I make my way to the terrace, I bump into Margaret and Richard, the couple I met the day before on the trip to the temples, and my eyes fill with tears of disappointment when I explain that Jack hasn\u2019t turned up. They tell me not to worry, pointing out that he had warned me he might be delayed, and insist that I spend the day with them. I tell them I\u2019d rather stay in the hotel for the next couple of hours in case Jack phones or suddenly turns up, but that I\u2019ll join them in the afternoon if he doesn\u2019t. I go up to my room and phone Adam. I\u2019m relieved when he doesn\u2019t pick up as it suits me to leave a message letting him know that Jack wasn\u2019t on the flight. Later, I go down to join Margaret and Richard, the strain of not having heard from Jack clearly visible on my face, especially when I tell them that I\u2019ve tried his mobile again several times without success. They are kindness itself and I\u2019m glad to have them to take my mind off things. I punctuate the time I spend with them with fruitless calls to Jack\u2019s mobile, urging him to phone me. In the evening, my new friends refuse to let me sit and mope alone so we have dinner together, where they talk brightly about how much they\u2019re looking forward to meeting Jack the following morning. I eventually get back to my room around midnight and find a message from Adam, saying he\u2019s sorry he missed my call and asking if I would like him to go over to the house to see if Jack is still there. I phone him back and tell him that yes, if he doesn\u2019t mind, but then we work out that if Jack is to catch the flight that evening, he will already have left for the airport. So I tell him not to bother and that I\u2019ll phone him the moment Jack arrives and we joke again about the telling-off he\u2019s going to get for worrying us all. The next morning, Margaret and Richard keep me company while I wait for Jack to arrive from the airport so they are there to witness my distress when he doesn\u2019t turn up. At Margaret\u2019s suggestion, I try to find out from British Airways if Jack was on the flight, but they are unable to help me, so I phone the British Embassy. I explain everything to them and maybe because Jack\u2019s name is known, they tell me they\u2019ll see what they can do. When they phone back and confirm that Jack wasn\u2019t on the flight, I burst into tears. I manage to pull myself together long enough to tell them that he doesn\u2019t seem to be at home either, but, although they are sympathetic, they tell me there isn\u2019t a lot they can do at this stage. They suggest I phone friends and relations in England to see if they know where he is and I thank them and hang up. With Margaret by my side, I call Adam and, my voice trembling with anxiety, tell him what has happened. He immediately offers to go straight round to the house and calls me back half an hour later to say that he\u2019s standing outside the gates, but that everything is shut up and nobody has answered the bell. So I worry that Jack has had an accident on the way to the airport and, although he reassures me, he says that he\u2019ll make some inquiries. I tell him that the British Embassy suggested I try to find out if anyone has spoken to him since I left and he offers to phone around for me. While I wait for Adam to get back to me, Diane calls to reassure me and to tell me that Adam is doing all he can to track Jack down. We talk for a while and, after I\u2019ve hung up, Margaret begins to ask me gentle questions and it dawns on me that she and Richard are wondering if there could be someone else in Jack\u2019s life, someone who he might have run off with. Horrified, I tell her that it had never occurred to me, because there had never been anything in his behaviour to suggest that there was, but that I suppose it\u2019s a possibility I\u2019m going to have to consider. The phone rings again. \u2018Grace?\u2019 \u2018Hello, Adam.\u2019 I make my voice hesitant, as if I\u2019m dreading what he\u2019s going to tell me. \u2018Have you managed to find out anything?\u2019 \u2018Only that Jack hasn\u2019t been admitted to any of the hospitals I phoned, which is good news.\u2019 \u2018It is,\u2019 I agree, giving a sigh of relief. \u2018On the other hand, I phoned as many people as I could think of but no one seems to have heard from him, at least not over the last few days. So I\u2019m afraid we\u2019re back to square one, really.\u2019 I look at Margaret, who nods encouragingly. \u2018There\u2019s something I need to ask you, Adam,\u2019 I say. \u2018Go on.\u2019 \u2018Is it possible that Jack was having an affair, maybe with someone at the office?\u2019 My words come out in a rush. \u2018An affair? Jack?\u2019 Adam sounds shocked. \u2018No, of course not. He would never do anything like that. He barely looked at another woman before he met you and he certainly hasn\u2019t since. You must know that, Grace.\u2019 Margaret, who gets the gist, gives my hand a squeeze. \u2018I do,\u2019 I say, chastened. \u2018It\u2019s just that I can\u2019t think of any other reason he would suddenly disappear without trace.\u2019 \u2018Can you think of any other friends he has, people that maybe I don\u2019t know?\u2019 \u2018Not really,\u2019 I say. \u2018Wait a minute, what about Moira and Giles, you know, the people who were at Millie\u2019s party. Maybe you could contact them. I don\u2019t have their number, though.\u2019 \u2018Leave it with me. What\u2019s their surname?\u2019 \u2018Kilburn-Hawes, I think.\u2019 \u2018I\u2019ll give them a ring and get back to you,\u2019 he promises. He calls back half an hour later and, when he tells me that they haven\u2019t heard from Jack either, I become distraught. Nobody seems to know what to do. The general consensus\u2014from Margaret, Richard, Adam and Diane\u2014is that it\u2019s too early to launch a missing person\u2019s inquiry so they tell me that the best thing would be to try to get some sleep and see if Jack turns up the next morning. He doesn\u2019t. The day passes in a blur as Mr Ho, Margaret, Richard and Adam take over. I tell them I want to go home, but they persuade me to stay for one more day in case Jack turns up, so I do. In the early afternoon\u2014eight o\u2019clock in the morning in England\u2014Adam calls to say that he has spoken to the local police and that, with my permission, they\u2019ll be happy to break into the house to see if they can find anything to indicate where Jack might have gone. They call me first and ask me to run through the last time I saw Jack and I tell them it was when Esther came to pick me up to take me to the airport, that he had waved me off from the study window. I explain that he hadn\u2019t been able to drive me to the airport himself because he\u2019d had quite a large whisky when he\u2019d come in from work and add that I hadn\u2019t particularly wanted to leave for Thailand by myself even though Jack had warned me, when the Tomasin case began to look as if it would overrun, that I might have to. They say they\u2019ll get back to me as soon as they can and I sit in my room and wait for them to phone with Margaret by my side, holding my hand. I know the news I\u2019m waiting for is going to be a long time coming so after a while I tell Margaret that I\u2019d like to try to sleep, and lie down on the bed. I manage to sleep until the moment I\u2019ve been waiting for since I arrived in Thailand finally comes. It begins with a knock on the door and, because I don\u2019t move, Margaret goes to answer it. I hear a man\u2019s voice and then Margaret comes over to the bed and, with a hand on my shoulder, gives me a little shake, telling me that there\u2019s someone to see me. As I sit up, I see her slip out of the room and I want to call her back, to tell her not to leave me, but he is already walking towards me so it\u2019s too late. My heart is beating so fast, my breathing so shallow that I don\u2019t dare look at him until I\u2019ve managed to compose myself. With my eyes fixed firmly on the ground, it\u2019s his shoes I see first. They are made of good leather and are well polished, just as I would expect them to be. He says my name and, as my eyes travel upwards, I see that while his suit is dark, in keeping with the occasion, it\u2019s made of a lightweight fabric, because of the climate. My eyes reach his face; it is pleasant, but grave, just as it should be. \u2018Mrs Angel?\u2019 he says again. \u2018Yes?\u2019 There\u2019s a trace of anxiousness in my voice. \u2018My name is Alastair Strachan. I\u2019m from the British Embassy.\u2019 He turns, and I see a young woman standing behind him. \u2018And this is Vivienne Dashmoor. I wonder if we could have a word?\u2019 I jump to my feet. \u2018Is it to do with Jack, have you managed to find him?\u2019 \u2018Yes\u2014or rather, the police in England have.\u2019 Relief floods my face. \u2018Thank goodness for that! Where is he? Why wasn\u2019t he answering his phone? Is he on his way here?\u2019 \u2018Perhaps we could go and sit down?\u2019 the young woman suggests. \u2018Of course,\u2019 I say, ushering them through to the sitting room. I sit down on the sofa and they take the armchairs. \u2018So where is he?\u2019 I ask. \u2018I mean, is he on his way here?\u2019 Mr Strachan clears his throat. \u2018I\u2019m very sorry to have to tell you this, Mrs Angel, but I\u2019m afraid that Mr Angel has been found dead.\u2019 I stare at him, my eyes wide with shock. Confusion floods my face. \u2018I don\u2019t understand,\u2019 I stammer. He shifts uncomfortably. \u2018I\u2019m afraid your husband has been found dead, Mrs Angel.\u2019 I shake my head vigorously. \u2018No, he can\u2019t be, he\u2019s coming here, to join me, he said he would. Where is he?\u2019 My voice trembles with emotion. \u2018I want to know where he is. Why isn\u2019t he here?\u2019 \u2018Mrs Angel, I know this is very difficult for you, but we need to ask you some questions,\u2019 the young lady says. \u2018Would you like us to fetch someone\u2014your friend, perhaps?\u2019 \u2018Yes, yes.\u2019 I nod. \u2018Can you get Margaret, please?\u2019 Mr Strachan goes to the door. I hear the murmur of voices and Margaret comes in. I see the shock on her face and I begin shaking uncontrollably. \u2018They\u2019re saying that Jack\u2019s dead,\u2019 I say. \u2018But he can\u2019t be, he can\u2019t be.\u2019 \u2018It\u2019s all right,\u2019 she murmurs, sitting down next to me and putting her arm around me. \u2018It\u2019s all right.\u2019 \u2018Perhaps we could have some tea brought up,\u2019 the young woman says, getting to her feet. She goes over to the phone and speaks to someone in reception. \u2018Did he have a car crash?\u2019 I ask Margaret, sounding bewildered. \u2018Is that what happened? Did Jack have a car crash on the way to the airport? Is that why he\u2019s not here?\u2019 \u2018I don\u2019t know,\u2019 she says quietly. \u2018He must have,\u2019 I go on, nodding with conviction. \u2018He must have been rushing to catch the flight, he must have left the house late and was driving too fast and had a crash. That\u2019s what happened, isn\u2019t it?\u2019 Margaret glances at Mr Strachan. \u2018I don\u2019t know, I\u2019m afraid.\u2019 My teeth begin chattering. \u2018I\u2019m cold.\u2019 She jumps to her feet, glad of something to do. \u2018Would you like a jumper? Is there one in your wardrobe?\u2019 \u2018Yes, I think so, not a jumper, a cardigan, maybe. The bathrobe, can I have the bathrobe?\u2019 \u2018Yes, of course.\u2019 She goes into the bathroom, finds the bathrobe, comes back and puts it around my shoulders. \u2018Thank you,\u2019 I murmur gratefully. \u2018Is that better?\u2019 she asks. \u2018Yes. But Jack can\u2019t be dead, it must be a mistake, it has to be.\u2019 She\u2019s saved from saying anything by a knock at the door. The young woman opens it and Mr Ho comes in, followed by a girl pushing a laden tea trolley. \u2018If I can be of further assistance, please let me know,\u2019 Mr Ho says quietly. I sense him looking at me as he leaves the room, but I keep my head bowed. The young woman busies herself with the tea and asks me if I would like sugar. \u2018No, thank you.\u2019 She places a cup and saucer in front of me and I pick up the cup, but I\u2019m shaking so much some of the tea slops over the side and onto my hand. Scalded, I clatter the cup back down onto the saucer. \u2018Sorry,\u2019 I say. Tears fill my eyes. \u2018I\u2019m sorry.\u2019 \u2018It\u2019s all right,\u2019 says Margaret hurriedly, taking a paper napkin and mopping my hand. I make an effort to pull myself together. \u2018I\u2019m sorry, I didn\u2019t catch your name,\u2019 I say to Mr Strachan. \u2018Alastair Strachan.\u2019 \u2018Mr Strachan, you say that my husband is dead.\u2019 I look at him for confirmation. \u2018Yes, I\u2019m afraid so.\u2019 \u2018Then can you please tell me how he died? I mean, was it quick, was anyone else hurt in the accident, where did it happen? I need to know, I need to know how it happened.\u2019 \u2018It wasn\u2019t a car accident, Mrs Angel.\u2019 \u2018Not a car accident?\u2019 I falter. \u2018Then how did he die?\u2019 Mr Strachan looks uncomfortable. \u2018I\u2019m afraid there\u2019s no easy way of saying this, Mrs Angel, but it seems that your husband took his own life.\u2019 And I burst into tears. \n PAST Once I\u2019d realised that I could get away with murder, I spent the rest of the night working out the details, thinking of ways to get Jack exactly where I needed him to be when the time came. Because my plan hinged on him losing the Tomasin case, I took a leaf out of his book and planned for every eventuality. I thought very carefully about what I would do if he won and, in the end, I decided that if he did I would drug him anyway and, while he was unconscious, phone the police. If I showed them the room in the basement, and the room where he kept me, maybe they would believe what I told them. In the event that I didn\u2019t manage to drug him before we left for the airport, I would somehow get the pills into him on the plane and try to get help once we arrived in Thailand. Neither solution was brilliant, but I didn\u2019t have any other options. Unless he lost. And, even then, there was no guarantee that he would bring up a glass of whisky to commiserate. The next day, the day of the verdict, I spent the morning crushing the remaining pills into as fine a powder as I possibly could and hid it in a screw of toilet paper, which I pushed into my sleeve as I would a tissue. When I eventually heard the whir of the black gates opening and the crunch of the gravel as Jack drove up to the front door sometime in the middle of the afternoon, my heart began hammering so hard I was afraid it would burst out of my chest. The time had finally come. Whether he had won or lost, I was going to have to act. He came into the hall, closed the front door and activated the shutters. I heard him open the cloakroom door, walk across the hall to the kitchen, followed by the familiar sounds of the freezer door opening and closing, the ice cubes being popped from the tray, the cupboard door opening and closing, the clink as the ice cubes were dropped into one glass\u2014I held my breath\u2014two glasses. His footsteps as he came up the stairs were heavy and told me all I needed to know. I began rubbing my left eye furiously so that by the time he unlocked the door it would be red and inflamed. \u2018Well?\u2019 I asked. \u2018How did it go?\u2019 He held out a glass to me. \u2018We lost.\u2019 \u2018Lost?\u2019 I said, taking it. Without bothering to answer, he raised his glass to his lips and, scared he would knock the whole lot back before I\u2019d had a chance to drug him, I jumped off the bed. \u2018I\u2019ve had something in my eye all morning,\u2019 I explained, blinking rapidly. \u2018Could you have a look?\u2019 \u2018What?\u2019 \u2018Could you just look at my eye a moment? I think there must be a fly in there or something.\u2019 As he peered into my eye, which I kept half shut, I worked the paper holding the powder from my sleeve and into the palm of my hand. \u2018So what happened?\u2019 I asked, unscrewing it as best I could with my fingers. \u2018Dena Anderson screwed me over,\u2019 he said bitterly. \u2018Can you open your eye a bit more?\u2019 Keeping my movements small, I moved the glass I was holding in my other hand under the paper and shook the powder into it. \u2018I can\u2019t, it\u2019s too painful,\u2019 I told him, stirring the contents around with my finger. \u2018Can you do it? I\u2019ll hold your glass for you.\u2019 With a sigh of annoyance, he handed me his glass and pulled my eye open using both hands. \u2018I can\u2019t see anything.\u2019 \u2018If I had a mirror, I\u2019d be able to see for myself,\u2019 I grumbled. \u2018It doesn\u2019t matter, it\u2019ll probably work itself out.\u2019 He held out his hand for his glass and I gave him mine. \u2018What shall we drink to?\u2019 \u2018Revenge,\u2019 he said, grimly. I raised the glass I was holding. \u2018To revenge, then.\u2019 I knocked half of the whisky back and was gratified to see him doing the same. \u2018Nobody makes a fool out of me. Antony Tomasin is going to suffer for this too.\u2019 \u2018But he was innocent,\u2019 I protested, wondering how I was going to keep him talking until the pills took effect. \u2018What has that got to do with it?\u2019 As he raised his glass to take another drink, I was alarmed to see tiny white specks floating in the whisky. \u2018Do you know what the best part of my job is?\u2019 \u2018No, what?\u2019 I said quickly. \u2018Sitting opposite all those battered women and imagining it was me who had beaten them up.\u2019 He knocked the rest of his glass back. \u2018And the photos, all those lovely photos of their injuries\u2014I suppose you could call it one of the perks of the job.\u2019 Incensed, I raised my glass and before I could stop myself, I had thrown the rest of my whisky in his face. His roar of anger, plus the knowledge that I had acted too soon, almost paralysed me. But as he lunged towards me, his eyes shut tight against the sting of the whisky, I took advantage of his momentary blindness and pushed him as hard as I could. As he stumbled awkwardly against the bed, the few seconds before he righted himself were all that I needed. Slamming the door behind me, I ran down the stairs to the hall below, looking urgently for somewhere to hide, because I couldn\u2019t let him catch me, not just yet. Upstairs, the door crashed back against the wall and as he came pounding down the stairs, I headed for the cloakroom and climbed into the wardrobe, hoping to buy myself a few precious minutes. This time, there was no singsong in his voice as he called for me. Instead, he roared my name, promising such harm to me that I trembled from my hiding place behind the coats. Several minutes passed, and I imagined him in the sitting room, checking behind every piece of furniture. The waiting was unbearable but I knew that with every minute that passed, the chances of the pills taking effect increased. At last, I heard the unmistakable sound of his footsteps coming down the hall. My legs turned to jelly and as the cloakroom door opened, I found myself sliding to the floor. The silence that followed was terrifying; I knew he was there, outside the wardrobe and I knew he knew I was inside. But he seemed content to leave me to sweat, relishing no doubt in the fear emanating from every pore of my body. I don\u2019t know when it occurred to me that the wardrobe might have a key, but the thought that at any moment he could turn it in the lock and imprison me there made it impossible for me to breathe. If I couldn\u2019t put the next part of my plan into action, there would be no saving Millie. Blind with panic, I flung myself against the doors. They burst open and I fell into a crumpled heap at Jack\u2019s feet. His rage as he pulled me up by my hair was tangible, and afraid that he might harm me physically I began screaming for mercy, telling him I was sorry and begging him not to take me down to the basement, gabbling incoherently that I would do anything as long as he didn\u2019t lock me in there. The mention of the basement had the desired effect. As he dragged me back along the hall I struggled so hard that he had no choice but to pick me up, and I let myself go limp so he would think I had given up. I used the time it took for him to carry me to the room he had prepared so carefully for Millie to focus on what I needed to do, so that when he tried to throw me down I held onto him as hard as I could. Enraged, he tried to shake me off and as he cursed me loudly, the slur in his voice was all that I needed. Still keeping hold of him, I allowed myself to slide down his body towards the floor, and when I reached his knees, I yanked them towards me as hard as I could. His legs buckled immediately and as he swayed above me, I used every ounce of strength I possessed to send him crashing to the floor. Stunned by the fall, his body heavy from the pills, he lay without moving for a few precious seconds and before he could recover, I fled the room, slamming the door behind me. As I ran towards the stairs, I could hear him hammering on the door, yelling at me to let him out and the fury in his voice made me start sobbing with fright. Reaching the hall, I kicked the door that led to the basement with my foot, shutting it against the noise. Taking the stairs two at a time, I ran to my bedroom, retrieved the glasses from where we had thrown them and carried them down to the kitchen, trying to ignore Jack\u2019s desperate attempts to get out of the room below by focusing on what I needed to do. With shaking hands, I washed the glasses, dried them carefully and put them back in the cupboard. Hurrying back upstairs, I went to my bedroom, straightened the bed, removed the shampoo, sliver of soap and towel from the bathroom and carried them into Jack\u2019s bathroom. Stripping off my pyjamas I put them in the laundry basket, went into the bedroom where my clothes were kept and got dressed quickly. I opened the wardrobe and took a couple of pairs of shoes from their boxes, some underwear and a dress, went back to the master bedroom and placed them around the room. On returning to the dressing room, I picked up the case that Jack had made me pack the night before and went downstairs. I wasn\u2019t worried about getting out of the house\u2014I didn\u2019t need a key to open the front door\u2014but I was worried about how I was going to get to the airport without any money. I knew that Jack had probably hung the jacket he had worn that morning in the cloakroom, but I didn\u2019t want to rifle through his clothes for money and hoped I would come across some while I was looking for my passport and tickets. I opened the door of his study and turned on the light. When I saw both passports and tickets lying neatly on his desk, I almost cried with relief. There was an envelope beside them and, opening it, I found some baht. With the sleeve of my cardigan over my fingers, I slid open one of the drawers, but I couldn\u2019t find any money and I didn\u2019t dare rifle through the other drawers. Taking my ticket, passport and the baht with me, I went back into the hall and, because I couldn\u2019t get to the airport without money, I went into the cloakroom, found his jacket, opened his wallet as carefully as I could and took out four fifty pound notes. I was about to close his wallet when his business cards caught my eye and, remembering that at some point I would need to phone his office, I took one. Realising that I had no idea what the time was, I went back to the kitchen and looked at the clock on the microwave. I was alarmed to see that it was already half past four, around the time I would need to leave for the airport on a Friday night for a check in at seven. In all my careful planning I hadn\u2019t actually thought about how I would get to the airport\u2014I suppose I\u2019d had a vague idea of taking a taxi\u2014so it was galling to realise that I had no idea what number I should call to order one. Public transport was out\u2014the nearest train station was a fifteen-minute walk away and I was loath to draw attention to myself by wheeling a heavy case along the road and anyway, I doubted it would get me there in time. Aware that I was wasting precious time, I went back into the hall and picked up the phone, wondering if such a thing as an operator still existed. As I stood there wondering what number I should dial, Esther\u2019s came into my head and, hardly daring to believe that I had remembered it correctly, I called her, praying that she would pick up. \u2018Hello?\u2019 I took a deep breath. \u2018Esther, it\u2019s Grace. Am I disturbing you?\u2019 \u2018No, not at all. I was just listening to the radio actually\u2014apparently, Antony Tomasin was acquitted.\u2019 She paused a moment as if she wasn\u2019t quite sure what to say. \u2018I guess Jack must be disappointed.\u2019 My mind raced. \u2018Yes, I\u2019m afraid he is rather.\u2019 \u2018Are you all right, Grace? You sound a bit upset.\u2019 \u2018It\u2019s Jack,\u2019 I admitted. \u2018He says he can\u2019t leave for Thailand tonight as he has too much paperwork to do. When he booked the tickets, he thought the case would be over long before now but because of the new evidence, about Dena Anderson having a lover, it overran.\u2019 \u2018You must be so disappointed! But you can always go later, can\u2019t you?\u2019 \u2018That\u2019s just it. Jack wants me to go tonight, as planned, and says he\u2019ll join me on Tuesday, once he\u2019s got everything sorted out. I\u2019ve told him that I\u2019d rather wait for him, but he says it\u2019s stupid to waste both tickets. He\u2019ll have to buy a new one for Tuesday, you see.\u2019 \u2018I take it you don\u2019t want to go without him.\u2019 \u2018No, of course I don\u2019t.\u2019 I gave a shaky laugh. \u2018But in the mood he\u2019s in, maybe it would be better. I\u2019m meant to be phoning for a taxi to take me to the airport\u2014he can\u2019t take me because he had a hefty whisky when he came in. The trouble is, I don\u2019t have a number for one and I don\u2019t dare disturb Jack in his study and ask him if I can use the computer to look for one, so I was wondering if you knew of a local firm.\u2019 \u2018Do you want me to take you? The children are already home from school and Rufus worked from home today, so it wouldn\u2019t be a problem.\u2019 It was the last thing I wanted. \u2018It\u2019s very kind of you, but I can\u2019t ask you to drive to the airport on a Friday night,\u2019 I said hastily. \u2018I don\u2019t think it\u2019ll be that easy to get a taxi at such short notice. What time do you need to leave?\u2019 \u2018Well, as soon as possible, really,\u2019 I admitted reluctantly. \u2018I have to check in at seven.\u2019 \u2018Then you\u2019d better let me take you.\u2019 \u2018I\u2019d rather take a taxi. If you could just give me a number?\u2019 \u2018Look, I\u2019ll take you\u2014it really isn\u2019t any trouble. Anyway, it\u2019ll get me out of the dreaded bath-time.\u2019 \u2018No, it\u2019s fine.\u2019 \u2018Why won\u2019t you let me help you, Grace?\u2019 There was something about the way she said it that put me on my guard. \u2018I just think it\u2019s an awful imposition, that\u2019s all.\u2019 \u2018It isn\u2019t.\u2019 Her voice was firm. \u2018Have you got all your stuff ready?\u2019 \u2018Yes, we packed yesterday.\u2019 \u2018Then I\u2019ll just go and tell Rufus I\u2019m taking you to the airport and I\u2019ll be straight over\u2014say, fifteen minutes?\u2019 \u2018Great,\u2019 I told her. \u2018Thank you, Esther, I\u2019ll tell Jack.\u2019 I put the phone down, appalled at what I had just agreed to.
